claim: The ANOSPP amplicon panel is a genus-wide targeted sequencing panel to facilitate large-scale monitoring of Anopheles species diversity.
source: The ANOSPP amplicon panel is a genus-wide targeted sequencing panel to facilitate large-scale monitoring of Anopheles species diversity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the ANOSPP panel.

claim: The ANOSPP panel contains 62 nuclear amplicons.
source: Combining information from the 62 nuclear amplicons present in the ANOSPP panel allows for a more senstive and specific species assignment than single gene (e.g. COI) barcoding, which is desirable in the light of permeable species boundaries.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of nuclear amplicons in the panel.

claim: Combining information from the 62 nuclear amplicons allows for more sensitive and specific species assignment than single gene barcoding.
source: Combining information from the 62 nuclear amplicons present in the ANOSPP panel allows for a more senstive and specific species assignment than single gene (e.g. COI) barcoding, which is desirable in the light of permeable species boundaries.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract as a comparison between multi-locus and single-locus approaches.

claim: NNoVAE correctly classifies 98% of samples within the An. gambiae complex with over 80% amplicon coverage.
source: In tests on independent samples with over 80% amplicon coverage, NNoVAE correctly classifies to species level 98% of samples within the An. gambiae complex and 89% of samples outside the complex.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing the method on independent samples.

claim: NNoVAE correctly classifies 89% of samples outside the An. gambiae complex with over 80% amplicon coverage.
source: In tests on independent samples with over 80% amplicon coverage, NNoVAE correctly classifies to species level 98% of samples within the An. gambiae complex and 89% of samples outside the complex.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing the method on independent samples.

claim: NNoVAE identified unexpected species in Gabon when applied to over two thousand new samples.
source: We apply NNoVAE to over two thousand new samples from Burkina Faso and Gabon, identifying unexpected species in Gabon.
evidence: This is stated as a result of applying the method to new field samples.

claim: There are plans to analyse half a million mosquitoes in the next five years using NNoVAE.
source: NNoVAE presents an approach that may be of value to other targeted sequencing panels, and is a method that will be used to survey Anopheles species diversity and Plasmodium transmission patterns through space and time on a large scale, with plans to analyse half a million mosquitoes in the next five years.
evidence: This is stated as a future plan in the abstract.

claim: The Anopheles genus contains nearly 500 formally described species.
source: The genus contains nearly 500 formally described species (Harbach and Kitching, 2016), which span more than 100 million years of evolution (Marinotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harbach and Kitching, 2016.

claim: The Anopheles genus spans more than 100 million years of evolution.
source: The genus contains nearly 500 formally described species (Harbach and Kitching, 2016), which span more than 100 million years of evolution (Marinotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marinotti et al., 2013.

claim: Only a subset of Anopheles species has the ability to transmit human malaria.
source: Only a subset of these species has the ability to transmit human malaria; however this vectorial capacity is not limited to a specific part of the species tree, but found throughout the genus phylogeny.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Anopheles species.

claim: Vectorial capacity for human malaria is found throughout the Anopheles genus phylogeny, not limited to a specific part of the species tree.
source: Only a subset of these species has the ability to transmit human malaria; however this vectorial capacity is not limited to a specific part of the species tree, but found throughout the genus phylogeny.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the distribution of vectorial capacity in the genus.

claim: Many Anopheles species are members of closely related species complexes or groups that are morphologically indistinguishable.
source: Many species are members of closely related species complexes or groups, which are morphologically indistinguishable and share large amounts of genetic variation due to their ability to hybridise in areas of sympatry (Anopheles gambiae 1000 Genomes Consortium, 2017; Harbach and Kitching, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Closely related Anopheles species share large amounts of genetic variation due to their ability to hybridise in areas of sympatry.
source: Many species are members of closely related species complexes or groups, which are morphologically indistinguishable and share large amounts of genetic variation due to their ability to hybridise in areas of sympatry (Anopheles gambiae 1000 Genomes Consortium, 2017; Harbach and Kitching, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Closely related Anopheles species may differ in vectorial capacity, insecticide resistance status and behavioural traits.
source: This is because even closely related species may differ in vectorial capacity, insecticide resistance status and behavioural traits, all of which can influence the efficacy of malaria control efforts (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to White et al., 2011.

claim: Differences in vectorial capacity, insecticide resistance status and behavioural traits can influence the efficacy of malaria control efforts.
source: This is because even closely related species may differ in vectorial capacity, insecticide resistance status and behavioural traits, all of which can influence the efficacy of malaria control efforts (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to White et al., 2011.

claim: Gene drive control efforts for An. gambiae are likely to be implemented this decade.
source: Novel control efforts like gene drive are likely to be implemented this decade for An. gambiae, and the success of these efforts will need to be closely monitored.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction about future malaria control implementation.

claim: The typical process of species identification for Anopheles mosquitoes starts by assigning them to species complexes or groups using morphological keys.
source: Currently, the typical process of species identification for Anopheles mosquitoes starts by assigning them to species complexes or groups using morphological keys (Gillies and Meillon, 1968; Gillies and Coetzee, 1987; Rattanarithikul and Panthusiri, 1994; Coetzee, 2020; Irish et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing morphological identification methods.

claim: Morphological keys for Anopheles identification are usually specific to geographical regions.
source: These morphological keys are usually specific to geographical regions and hence require in-depth and up-to-date knowledge of the species ranges.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of morphological identification methods.

claim: The accuracy of morphological classification depends on the level of experience and expertise of the person carrying out the identification.
source: Because the morphological features distinguishing one group of species from another can be very nuanced, the accuracy of morphological classification depends on the level of experience and expertise of the person carrying out the identification.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of morphological identification.

claim: Species inside species complexes can be morphologically indistinguishable from each other at the adult stage.
source: Species inside species complexes can be morphologically indistinguishable from each other at the adult stage and hence molecular assays are required for precise species identification.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for requiring molecular assays.

claim: The most commonly used molecular method for Anopheles species identification is a PCR-based species diagnostic assay targeting the internal transcribed spacer (ITS2) or similarly variable genomic regions.
source: The most commonly used method is a PCR-based species diagnostic assay, targeting the highly variable internal transcribed spacer (ITS2) or similarly variable genomic regions (Cohuet et al., 2003; Scott et al., 1993; Fanello et al., 2002; Wilkins et al., 2006), although other approaches exist, for example based on mass spectrometry (Nabet et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published methods.

claim: PCR assays for Anopheles species identification require the use of primers specific to the species complex or group.
source: The PCR assays require the use of primers specific to the species complex or group, hence higher level morphological misclassification can lead to failure to generate PCR product or even erroneous species classification (Erlank et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic and limitation of PCR-based methods, supported by a citation.

claim: Higher level morphological misclassification can lead to failure to generate PCR product or erroneous species classification.
source: The PCR assays require the use of primers specific to the species complex or group, hence higher level morphological misclassification can lead to failure to generate PCR product or even erroneous species classification (Erlank et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Erlank et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations in primer or restriction sites can lead to PCR failures.
source: Mutations in primer or restriction sites can also lead to PCR failures.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of PCR-based methods.

claim: The ANOSPP panel targets 62 loci in the generic Anopheles nuclear genome, spread over all chromosome arms.
source: In brief, the panel targets 62 loci in the generic Anopheles nuclear genome, spread over all chromosome arms, including exonic, intronic as well as intergenic regions.
evidence: This is a description of the panel design from Makunin et al., 2022.

claim: The ANOSPP panel targets two conserved loci on the generic Plasmodium mitochondrial genome.
source: Additionally, it targets two conserved loci on the generic Plasmodium mitochondrial genome, to simultaneously evaluate Plasmodium presence and species for each individual mosquito.
evidence: This is a description of the panel design from Makunin et al., 2022.

claim: The ANOSPP panel can use an extremely small aliquot of DNA (<1% of whole mosquito extraction) extracted from each mosquito.
source: Furthermore, the panel can use an extremely small aliquot of DNA (<1% of whole mosquito extraction) extracted from each mosquito using a cheap, nondestructive, high-throughput workflow (Makunin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the panel, supported by citation to Makunin et al., 2022.

claim: The ANOSPP panel uses a non-destructive extraction approach that preserves the mosquito carcass for morphological evaluation post-sequencing.
source: Ethanol is then added again to the mosquito carcass to preserve the mosquito and enable morphological evaluation of any individual post-sequencing.
evidence: This is described as part of the workflow.

claim: A single Illumina library containing amplified and bar-coded material pooled from 768 samples is sequenced on a single Illumina MiSeq lane.
source: A single Illumina library is generated containing amplified and bar-coded material pooled from 768 samples, then sequenced on a single Illumina MiSeq lane.
evidence: This is described as part of the sequencing workflow.

claim: NNoVAE is a k-mer-based method consisting of a Nearest Neighbours (NN) step and a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) step.
source: Here, we present a new species assignment method that we call NNoVAE, which is a k-mer-based method consisting of an initial step using Nearest Neighbours (NN) that identifies samples down to a species or, in some cases, a species complex, and a second step using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) for species identification within a species complex.
evidence: This is the description of the method presented in the paper.

claim: The NN step of NNoVAE assigns a sample to a species-group by comparing k-mers arising from each haplotype's amplicon sequence to a reference database.
source: The NN step assigns a sample to a species-group by comparing the k-mers arising from each haplotype's amplicon sequence to a reference database.
evidence: This is described in the abstract as part of the method.

claim: The VAE step is required to distinguish between closely related species within species complexes.
source: The VAE step is required to distinguish between closely related species, and also has sufficient resolution to reveal population structure within species.
evidence: This is stated as the purpose of the VAE step.

claim: The VAE step has sufficient resolution to reveal population structure within species.
source: The VAE step is required to distinguish between closely related species, and also has sufficient resolution to reveal population structure within species.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the VAE step.

claim: The reference database NNv1 contains 186 samples representing 62 species spread over 4 subgenera.
source: The reference database we constructed consists of well-curated samples sequenced with the panel, in silico extracted reference genomes, and in silico extracted whole genome short read data. As we expect that the reference database will expand to include additional species and populations over time, we assign a version number to the database. The reference database described here, which we call NNv1, contains 186 samples, representing 62 species spread over 4 subgenera.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the reference database composition.

claim: Samples required at least 10 targets amplified to be included in the reference database NNv1.
source: To maintain the advantages of multi-locus assignment, we required samples to have at least 10 targets amplified to be included in the reference database.
evidence: This is stated as a criterion for inclusion in the reference database.

claim: Six species in the An. gambiae complex have been included from publicly available whole genome data to increase resolution.
source: In addition, six species in the An. gambiae complex have been included from publicly available whole genome data (The Anopheles gambiae 1000 Genomes Consortium, 2021; Fontaine et al., 2015) in order to increase the resolution in a group of hard to distinguish species.
evidence: This is stated as part of the database construction, with citations to data sources.

claim: Three levels of species-groups were defined based on pairwise k-mer distances: fine (threshold 0.1), intermediate (threshold 0.3), and coarse (threshold 0.51).
source: For a threshold of 0.1 on the sample 8-mer distance, most species-groups satisfy or nearly satisfy the partitioning condition, and each species-group contains a single species or multiple species from a known species complex or group, for example An. gambiae and An. coluzzii are grouped together at the 0.1 threshold. We refer to the species-groups at the 0.1 level as the fine level species-groups and they are most useful for species assignment, because they provide the highest resolution. A threshold of 0.3 merges samples representing species from some well-known complexes, like the entire An. gambiae complex, into a single species-group. Similarly, many of the species for which we currently only have a single representative in the reference database NNv1, are merged into larger species-groups. We refer to this level of species-groups as the intermediate level, which provides insight into the degree of similarity between different fine level species-groups. Additionally, the intermediate level species-groups can be informative when we sequence a sample whose species is not represented in the database because the species assignment at the intermediate level places the sample within its most closely related species-group in the database. Thresholds higher than 0.3 tend to violate the partitioning condition to a greater extent, but it is desirable to include a coarse level classification to get an approximate taxonomic position of unrepresented species and of more diverged species. We selected 0.51 as a threshold for the coarse level classification because this gives reasonably clear species-groups that roughly correspond to taxonomic series.
evidence: This is described as the method for defining species-groups at different hierarchical levels.

claim: If the sample assignment proportion is at least 0.8 for one species-group, the sample is classified as a member of that group.
source: If the sample assignment proportion is at least 0.8 for one species-group, the sample is classified as a member of that group. If the classification threshold of 0.8 is not met at the chosen level, the sample remains unassigned at that level.
evidence: This is stated as the classification threshold used in the NN method.

claim: 61.8% of samples in the reference database were assigned correctly at the fine level in leave-one-out testing (excluding samples that form a species-group on their own).
source: If we ignore the samples that form a species-group on their own, because we do not yet have sufficient representation for those species, 61.8% of samples are assigned correctly at the fine level, and 98.8% and 100% at the intermediate and coarse level respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from leave-one-out testing on the reference database.

claim: 98.8% of samples in the reference database were assigned correctly at the intermediate level in leave-one-out testing (excluding samples that form a species-group on their own).
source: If we ignore the samples that form a species-group on their own, because we do not yet have sufficient representation for those species, 61.8% of samples are assigned correctly at the fine level, and 98.8% and 100% at the intermediate and coarse level respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from leave-one-out testing on the reference database.

claim: 100% of samples in the reference database were assigned correctly at the coarse level in leave-one-out testing (excluding samples that form a species-group on their own).
source: If we ignore the samples that form a species-group on their own, because we do not yet have sufficient representation for those species, 61.8% of samples are assigned correctly at the fine level, and 98.8% and 100% at the intermediate and coarse level respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from leave-one-out testing on the reference database.

claim: The An. gambiae complex classifier contains 7 out of 8 formally named species in the complex, as well as two putative cryptic species.
source: The classifier we present here contains 7 out of 8 formally named species in the complex (Coetzee et al., 2013), as well as two putative cryptic species (Tennessen et al., 2021; Barrón et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the classifier composition, with citations.

claim: The training set GCref v1 contains 406 An. gambiae, 222 An. coluzzii, 94 An. arabiensis, 11 An. quadriannulatus, 3 An. melas, 6 An. merus, 3 An. bwambae, 38 An. tengrela, and 4 An. fontenillei samples.
source: The species represented in GCref v1 are An. gambiae (406), An. coluzzii (222), An. arabiensis (94), An. quadriannulatus (11), An. melas (3), An.merus (6), An. bwambae (3), An. tengrela (38), and An. fontenillei (4).
evidence: This is stated as the composition of the training dataset.

claim: 97% of samples in GCref v1 have at least 55 of 62 targets amplified.
source: These samples are generally high coverage: 97% of samples have at least 55 of 62 targets amplified.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the training dataset quality.

claim: The validation set GCval v1 contains 80 An. gambiae, 15 An. coluzzii, 30 An. arabiensis, 1 An. melas, 5 An. merus, and 12 An. tengrela samples.
source: The species represented in GCval v1 are An. gambiae (80), An. coluzzii (15), An. arabiensis (30), An. melas (1), An. merus (5), and An. tengrela (12).
evidence: This is stated as the composition of the validation dataset.

claim: The VAE uses a three-dimensional latent space.
source: In our case, we use a three-dimensional latent space (d=3).
evidence: This is stated as a parameter choice for the VAE.

claim: 134 out of 142 samples (94.4%) in GCval v1 were assigned to a single species.
source: 134 out of 142 samples (94.4%) samples are assigned to a single species and 132 of those (98.5%) are assigned to the species concordant with their species label.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing the VAE classifier on the validation set.

claim: 132 out of 134 samples (98.5%) assigned to a single species in GCval v1 were assigned to the species concordant with their species label.
source: 134 out of 142 samples (94.4%) samples are assigned to a single species and 132 of those (98.5%) are assigned to the species concordant with their species label.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing the VAE classifier on the validation set.

claim: The Ag1000G project removes samples from its analysis that appear not to be An. gambiae, An. coluzzii, or An. arabiensis based on their divergence from the PEST reference genome.
source: The Ag1000G project removes samples from its analysis that appear not to be An. gambiae, An. coluzzii, or An. arabiensis based on their divergence from the PEST (An. gambiae) reference genome.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the Ag1000G project's quality control.

claim: 212 of nearly 10,000 samples in Ag1000G data releases v3 and v3.1 through v3.5 were filtered due to high divergence from the PEST reference genome.
source: In these datasets, 212 of nearly 10,000 samples were filtered due to high divergence from the PEST reference genome; we assign 166 of those to An. funestus at the fine level and 17 to the An. gambiae complex at the intermediate level.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying NNoVAE to Ag1000G filtered samples.

claim: 166 of the 212 Ag1000G diverged samples were assigned to An. funestus at the fine level.
source: In these datasets, 212 of nearly 10,000 samples were filtered due to high divergence from the PEST reference genome; we assign 166 of those to An. funestus at the fine level and 17 to the An. gambiae complex at the intermediate level.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying NNoVAE to Ag1000G filtered samples.

claim: 17 of the 212 Ag1000G diverged samples were assigned to the An. gambiae complex at the intermediate level.
source: In these datasets, 212 of nearly 10,000 samples were filtered due to high divergence from the PEST reference genome; we assign 166 of those to An. funestus at the fine level and 17 to the An. gambiae complex at the intermediate level.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying NNoVAE to Ag1000G filtered samples.

claim: Of the 17 Ag1000G samples assigned to the An. gambiae complex, 5 were assigned to An. merus, 11 to An. melas, and 1 to Uncertain_melas_quadriannulatus.
source: All 17 samples that are assigned to the An. gambiae complex had at least 50 targets. We assigned 5 samples to An. merus, 11 to An. melas and 1 to Uncertain_melas_quadriannulatus (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the VAE classifier to Ag1000G samples.

claim: 950 mosquitoes were collected from three different locations in Burkina Faso.
source: We collected 950 mosquitoes from three different locations in Burkina Faso.
evidence: This is stated as the sample collection for the Burkina Faso case study.

claim: All individuals from Burkina Faso were morphologically assigned to the An. gambiae complex.
source: All individuals were morphologically assigned to the An. gambiae complex.
evidence: This is stated as the morphological identification result for Burkina Faso samples.

claim: 905 individuals (95.3%) from Burkina Faso obtained at least 10 amplified targets.
source: For 905 individuals (95.3%) we obtained at least 10 amplified targets, the minimum number required for NN assignment.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequencing Burkina Faso samples.

claim: 901 samples from Burkina Faso were assigned to the An. gambiae complex at the intermediate level.
source: A total of 901 samples are indeed assigned to the An.gambiae complex at the intermediate level, 2 samples are assigned to An. nili group sp3 at the fine level, 1 sample could only be assigned at the coarse level to the Myzomyia Neocellia series and 1 sample could not be assigned at any level.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying NNoVAE to Burkina Faso samples.

claim: Three species were found in the Burkina Faso dataset: An. gambiae, An. coluzzii, and An. arabiensis.
source: We find three species in this dataset: An. gambiae, An. coluzzii, and An. arabiensis (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a result and shown in Figure 5.

claim: 91.6% of Burkina Faso samples with at least 50 amplified targets could be assigned to a single species.
source: Most samples (91.6%) could be assigned to a single species, but we also find some samples labelled as uncertain shared between An. gambiae and one other species.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the VAE classifier to Burkina Faso samples.

claim: 1,056 mosquitoes were collected by human landing catch from different locations in Lopé village in Gabon.
source: We collected 1,056 mosquitoes by human landing catch from different locations in Lopé village in Gabon.
evidence: This is stated as the sample collection for the Gabon case study.

claim: All individuals from Gabon were morphologically identified as members of the An. gambiae complex.
source: All individuals were morphologically identified as members of the An. gambiae complex.
evidence: This is stated as the morphological identification result for Gabon samples.

claim: Eleven mosquitoes from Gabon were identified as An. fontenillei by a species diagnostic PCR.
source: Eleven mosquitoes were identified as An. fontenillei by a species diagnostic PCR (Fanello et al., 2002) and those clustered with the An. fontenillei and An. bwambae samples in the VAE projection as expected.
evidence: This is stated as a result from PCR identification, with citation.

claim: 1002 (95.9%) of the unidentified Gabon samples obtained at least 10 targets.
source: For 1002 (95.9%) of the unidentified samples we obtain at least 10 targets and these are classified by the NN step of NNoVAE.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequencing Gabon samples.

claim: 993 samples (99.1%) from Gabon were assigned to the An. gambiae complex.
source: The vast majority (993 samples; 99.1%) is assigned to the An. gambiae complex.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying NNoVAE to Gabon samples.

claim: Two An. funestus individuals and two An. coustani complex individuals were found in the Gabon dataset.
source: The other species we find in this dataset are An. funestus (two individuals) and An. coustani complex (two individuals), plus five individuals that could not be assigned at any level.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying NNoVAE to Gabon samples.

claim: 890 (89.6%) of the 993 Gabon mosquitoes assigned to the An. gambiae complex have sufficiently many targets to be run through the VAE.
source: Of the 993 mosquitoes assigned to the An. gambiae complex, 890 (89.6%) have sufficiently many targets to be run through the VAE (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from processing Gabon samples.

claim: 632 Gabon samples were assigned to An. coluzzii, 130 to An. gambiae, and 1 to An. fontenillei.
source: Most of these are assigned to a single species: 632 to An. coluzzii, 130 An. gambiae, and 1 An. fontenillei (the latter is actually assigned to the combined convex hull of An. fontenillei and An. bwambae, but are assumed to be An. fontenillei because of the non-overlapping species ranges).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the VAE classifier to Gabon samples.

claim: Four samples from Gabon were projected close to the An. arabiensis cluster and confirmed as An. arabiensis by independent PCR species diagnostics.
source: Four other samples are projected close to the An. arabiensis cluster, although they are assigned to a large set of species labels. Independent PCR species diagnostics confirmed these four samples as An. arabiensis (Fanello et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a result confirmed by independent PCR, with citation.

claim: An. arabiensis has not been observed in Gabon before, despite extensive sampling efforts.
source: This was surprising because An. arabiensis has not been observed in Gabon before, despite extensive sampling efforts.
evidence: This is stated as context for the significance of finding An. arabiensis in Gabon.

claim: An. fontenillei was first discovered in the forest of La Lopé National Park, 10–15 km south of the Gabon sampling locations.
source: An. fontenillei was first discovered in the forest of La Lopé National Park, 10–15 km south of the sampling locations presented in this study (Barrón et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation.

claim: The VAE projection of the An. gambiae complex shows geographical structure within species clusters.
source: In addition to structure driven by species, the latent space projection of GCref v1 also exhibits geographical structure. Within the An. gambiae species cluster, there is a distinct subcluster of samples from Madagascar. Similarly, there is a distinct subcluster of samples from Madagascar in the An. arabiensis species cluster.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the VAE projection.

claim: There is a distinct subcluster of samples from Madagascar in the An. gambiae species cluster.
source: Within the An. gambiae species cluster, there is a distinct subcluster of samples from Madagascar.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the VAE projection.

claim: There is a distinct subcluster of samples from Madagascar in the An. arabiensis species cluster.
source: Similarly, there is a distinct subcluster of samples from Madagascar in the An. arabiensis species cluster.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the VAE projection.

claim: The boundary between the An. gambiae and An. coluzzii species clusters is formed by samples from the far West of Africa.
source: As mentioned before, the boundary between the An. gambiae and An. coluzzii species clusters is formed by samples from the far West of Africa.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the VAE projection.

claim: Samples from The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau that form the boundary between An. gambiae and An. coluzzii cannot be confidently assigned to either species using over 500 ancestry informative markers or whole genome PCA.
source: Interestingly, the boundary is formed by mosquitoes from The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau. These mosquitoes are labelled as An. gambiae by conventional molecular barcoding, but they cannot be confidently assigned to either An. gambiae or An. coluzzii using over 500 ancestry informative markers (AIMs) or whole genome PCA (Anopheles gambiae 1000 Genomes Consortium, 2017; Clarkson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claim: An. bwambae and An. fontenillei clusters are placed very close to each other in the VAE projection and cannot be reliably distinguished.
source: The clusters containing An. bwambae and the putative new species An. fontenillei are placed very close to each other, and can also not be reliably distinguished.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the VAE projection.

claim: An. bwambae and An. fontenillei do not seem to have overlapping geographic species ranges.
source: These species are closely related, but up until now they have only been discovered in Uganda and Gabon, respectively, and so, since they do not seem to have overlapping geographic species ranges (Barrón et al., 2019), the species identity of samples falling into either of these two clusters can be resolved by their geographic origin.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Barrón et al., 2019.

claim: K-mer based distances naturally incorporate indels and structural variation.
source: K-mer based distances naturally incorporate indels and structural variation and account for highly diverged sequences in an objective way and provide a solution to the problems arising from relying on alignments.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of k-mer based methods.

claim: 8-mers were selected as a reasonable k-mer length for the analysis.
source: Based on these trade-offs, we selected 8-mers as a reasonable length.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice.

claim: The total sequence length of the amplicon panel targets for the An. gambiae PEST reference genome sequence AgamP4 is 9928 bp.
source: The total sequence length of the amplicon panel targets for the current An. gambiae PEST reference genome sequence AgamP4 is 9928 bp, with a mean target length of 160 bp.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the amplicon panel.

claim: The mean target length of the amplicon panel is 160 bp.
source: The total sequence length of the amplicon panel targets for the current An. gambiae PEST reference genome sequence AgamP4 is 9928 bp, with a mean target length of 160 bp.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the amplicon panel.

claim: The chance that all 8-mers within a target are unique is 84% on average.
source: There are 65536 unique 8-mers, so the chance that all 8-mers within a target are unique is 84% on average.
evidence: This is stated as a calculated probability based on target length.

claim: The expected number of unique 8-mers across the nearly 10 kb of amplified sequence is approximately 8533 (sd 46).
source: Across the nearly 10 kb of amplified sequence, the chance that all 8-mers are unique is vanishingly small, but the expected number of unique 8-mers is approximately 8533 (sd 46) and the expected number of non-unique 8-mers is approximately 680 (sd 22).
evidence: This is stated as a calculated expectation.

claim: Version 2 of the reference database is expected to contain approximately fifty additional species.
source: We expect that version 2 of the reference database will contain approximately fifty additional species, as well as more individuals of species that are underrepresented in NNv1 and we are seeking further well-characterised samples.
evidence: This is stated as a future plan for database expansion.

claim: The goal over the next 2 years is to adapt the ANOSPP protocol to run in any basic molecular laboratory.
source: Our goal over the next 2 years is to adapt the ANOSPP protocol, which currently uses high-throughput robotics equipment at Sanger, to run it in any basic molecular laboratory.
evidence: This is stated as a future goal.

claim: There are plans to build an accompanying website where sequence data will be automatically accessible and data analyses can be run interactively and openly.
source: We plan to build an accompanying website where sequence data will be automatically accessible and data analyses can be run interactively and openly (if desired).
evidence: This is stated as a future plan.

claim: By successfully targeting a single vector species, a different species can become the main transmitter of malaria.
source: It has been shown that by successfully targeting a single vector species, a different species can become the main transmitter of malaria (Okumu and Finda, 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Okumu and Finda, 2021.

claim: An. stephensi, originally found in South East Asia and the Arabian peninsula, has been reported to spread in the Horn of Africa.
source: An. stephensi, an efficient vector species originally found in South East Asia and the Arabian peninsula, has been reported to spread in the Horn of Africa and was implicated in malaria outbreaks in Djibouti (Faulde et al., 2014; Seyfarth et al., 2019; Ahmed et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published reports.

claim: An. stephensi was implicated in malaria outbreaks in Djibouti.
source: An. stephensi, an efficient vector species originally found in South East Asia and the Arabian peninsula, has been reported to spread in the Horn of Africa and was implicated in malaria outbreaks in Djibouti (Faulde et al., 2014; Seyfarth et al., 2019; Ahmed et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published reports.

claim: The amplicon sequencing data are processed by splitting fastq files into one file per target using cutadapt v2.5.
source: In brief, the fastq files containing the reads are split into one file per target by cutadapt v2.5 (Martin, 2011), which uses the primer sequences to do so.
evidence: This is described as part of the data processing pipeline, with citation.

claim: DADA2 v1.10 is used to reconstruct sample haplotypes from read pairs.
source: Next, DADA2 v1.10 (Callahan et al., 2016) is used to reconstruct sample haplotypes from these read pairs and they are filtered using a custom script to include only haplotypes supported by at least 10 read pairs and with at least 0.1 haplotype frequency per sample-amplicon pair.
evidence: This is described as part of the data processing pipeline, with citation.

claim: Haplotypes are filtered to include only those supported by at least 10 read pairs and with at least 0.1 haplotype frequency per sample-amplicon pair.
source: Next, DADA2 v1.10 (Callahan et al., 2016) is used to reconstruct sample haplotypes from these read pairs and they are filtered using a custom script to include only haplotypes supported by at least 10 read pairs and with at least 0.1 haplotype frequency per sample-amplicon pair.
evidence: This is described as a filtering criterion in the data processing pipeline.

claim: In silico amplicon extraction from reference genomes is done by matching primer sequences in the reference genome using SeekDeep v2.6 command 'genTargetInfoFromGenomes'.
source: Targets are extracted by matching the primer sequences in the reference genome using SeekDeep v2.6 command 'genTargetInfoFromGenomes' (Hathaway et al., 2018).
evidence: This is described as the method for in silico extraction, with citation.

claim: The coarse level threshold of 0.51 groups together the Myzomyia and Neocellia series in the Cellia subgenus.
source: However, it is not perfect, as it groups together the Myzomyia and Neocellia series in the Cellia subgenus and it splits the Neomyzomyia series into three distinct species-groups.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the coarse level classification.

claim: The coarse level threshold of 0.51 splits the Neomyzomyia series into three distinct species-groups.
source: However, it is not perfect, as it groups together the Myzomyia and Neocellia series in the Cellia subgenus and it splits the Neomyzomyia series into three distinct species-groups.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the coarse level classification.

claim: A similar effect of the Neomyzomyia series not forming a monophyletic clade was observed in Makunin et al., 2022.
source: A similar effect was observed in Makunin et al., 2022, where the Neomyzomyia series did not form a monophyletic clade.
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: On average 1.2% of targets per sample in the NNv1 reference database have more than two different sequences.
source: In the NNv1 reference database on average 1.2% of targets per sample have more than two different sequences; in the query datasets discussed later in this article this percentage ranged from 0.3% to 2.3%.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the data.

claim: In the query datasets, the percentage of targets with more than two different sequences ranged from 0.3% to 2.3%.
source: In the NNv1 reference database on average 1.2% of targets per sample have more than two different sequences; in the query datasets discussed later in this article this percentage ranged from 0.3% to 2.3%.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the data.

claim: The VAE projection shows that samples from The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau stand out as a separate group in whole genome data studies.
source: These samples also stand out as a separate group in a study on whole genome data (Caputo et al., 2021; Clarkson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to published studies.

claim: There appears to be a cluster of East African An. gambiae samples that are distinct from the main cluster of An. gambiae as well as the Madagascar samples.
source: There also appears to be a cluster of East African An. gambiae samples that are distinct from the main cluster of An. gambiae as well as the Madagascar samples.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the VAE projection.

claim: The amplicon panel can be useful to explore population structure within species.
source: It is promising to see signatures of geographic structure within species from the amplicon panel data, because this suggests that the panel can also be useful to explore population structure within species.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from observed geographic structure.

claim: The presence or absence of samples from The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau affects the VAE classification accuracy to distinguish between An. gambiae and An. coluzzii.
source: We observed that the presence or absence of most countries does not affect the classification, except for the Gambia and Guinea-Bissau. When these countries are removed, the accuracy to distinguish between An. gambiae and An. coluzzii considerably reduces.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from testing the effect of training dataset composition.

claim: Samples from The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau lie on the boundary of the An. gambiae and An. coluzzii clusters and are crucial for assigning those species.
source: This is not surprising, since these samples lie on the boundary of the An. gambiae and An. coluzzii clusters and as such are crucial for assigning those species.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the importance of these samples.

claim: Figure 1 shows the pairwise k-mer distances between all samples in the reference database.
source: Figure 1 shows the pairwise k-mer distances between all samples in the reference database.
evidence: This is a description of what Figure 1 displays.

claim: Dark triangles below the diagonal in Figure 1 reflect that samples of the same or closely related species have a smaller 8-mer distance to each other than to other samples.
source: One can observe dark triangles below the diagonal, reflecting that samples of the same or closely related species have a smaller 8-mer distance to each other than to other samples.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the pattern in Figure 1.

claim: Figure 2 shows two examples of the nearest neighbour assignment of test samples Amou-3-2 (An. moucheti) and Agam-35 (An. gambiae).
source: Figure 2 shows two examples of the nearest neighbour assignment of a test sample. The test samples are Amou-3–2 and Agam-35, an An. moucheti and An. gambiae individual, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of what Figure 2 displays.

claim: For sample Amou-3-2, for most targets, the nearest neighbour sequence is found in all four An. moucheti samples in the reference database.
source: For Amou-3–2 we see that for most targets, the nearest neighbour sequence is found in all four An. moucheti samples in the reference database NNv1.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 2.

claim: For sample Agam-35, for many targets, the nearest neighbour sequences are found not only in An_gambiae_coluzzii samples, but also in samples from other species in the An. gambiae complex.
source: For Agam-35 the heatmap shows that, for many targets, the nearest neighbour sequences are not only found in An_gambiae_coluzzii samples, but also in samples from other species in the An. gambiae complex.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 2.

claim: Sample Agam-35 cannot be classified with sufficient confidence to a single species at the fine level.
source: At the fine level, the largest assignment proportion is to the An_gambiae_coluzzii species-group, but it does not meet the 0.8 classification threshold because of the relatively high assignment proportions to other species-groups within the An. gambiae complex. So at the fine level, this sample cannot be classified with sufficient confidence to a single species.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the assignment results for Agam-35.

claim: The average correct assignment proportion per sample at the coarse level is 99.4% for samples of species that are well-represented in the reference database.
source: For the same group of samples, the average correct assignment proportion per sample at the coarse level is 99.4%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from leave-one-out testing.

claim: The average correct assignment proportion per sample at the intermediate level is 95.8% for samples of species that are well-represented in the reference database.
source: And in fact, the average correct assignment proportion of 95.8% at the intermediate level shows that these assignments are also generally with high confidence.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from leave-one-out testing.

claim: The average correct assignment proportion per sample at the fine level is 81.3% for samples of species that are well-represented in the reference database.
source: At the fine level the confidence starts to break down for some samples, in particular the An. gambiae complex, which is represented by many samples in the reference database. Then the average correct assignment per sample is 81.3%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from leave-one-out testing.

claim: 21 species-groups at the fine level in NNv1 consist of a single sample.
source: In NNv1, 21 species-groups at the fine level consist of a single sample.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the reference database composition.

claim: Four samples in the reference database could not be classified in leave-one-out testing: An. christyi, An. atroparvus, An. oryzalimnetes, and An. cruzii.
source: The four unclassified samples are An. christyi, An. atroparvus, An. oryzalimnetes, and An. cruzii.
evidence: This is stated as a result from leave-one-out testing.

claim: The Kerteszia and Nyssorhynchus subgenera are underrepresented in the reference database, both in number of species and number of samples.
source: In particular, the Kerteszia and Nyssorhynchus subgenus are underrepresented, both in number of species and number of samples, but also the basal species in for instance the Pyretophorus series are not well represented and are too diverged from the other species in this series to exhibit strong similarity to the other samples from this series.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current reference database.
